title: An operations engineer's first day
audience: Someone who runs systems and changes them carefully.

steps.see: A summary of the project, its runbook, recent incidents and open tasks.
steps.why: You start from the written state of the system, not from memory.

steps.see: Overdue tasks with how many days late and who is waiting.
steps.why: Late rotations and renewals show up before they bite.

steps.goal: Check a claim before you act
steps.say: /gt:gt-validate the certificate on the order service expires on 2026-12-01
steps.see: A fresh reviewer checks the claim against the rules and the artifact and reports confirmed, refuted or unknown.
steps.why: A number that matters is verified by something that did not make it up.

steps.goal: Write the steps down while they are fresh
steps.see: The commands, gotchas and the incident summary go to the runbook and the project's findings.
steps.why: The next on-call person finds the fix instead of rediscovering it.

steps.see: A handoff note: what is done, what is half-done, and what to verify first.
steps.why: Whoever picks this up knows what is true and what is only believed.

steps.see: The notes saved, tasks updated and the session's claim on the vault released.
steps.why: Nothing is left half-written and nobody else is blocked.
